name: Niccolò Barbaro
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: Witnessed and recorded the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

name: Sultan Mehmed II
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: Captured Constantinople in 1453, destroying the Byzantine Empire.

name: Mansa Musa
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: Renowned for his immense gold wealth and famous pilgrimage to Mecca.

name: Admiral Zheng He
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: Commanded massive Chinese treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean.

name: Christopher Columbus
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: His 1492 voyage to the Americas initiated European global expansion.

name: Martin Luther
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: His 1517 protests sparked the Protestant Reformation, dividing Europe.

name: Pope Alexander VI
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: Issued the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas dividing the Americas between Spain and Portugal.

name: King Philip II
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: Catholic monarch who launched the Spanish Armada against England.

name: Queen Elizabeth I
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: Protestant Queen who authorized privateers and defeated the Spanish Armada.

name: Mary, Queen of Scots
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: Catholic monarch whose execution angered Philip II.

name: Henry VIII
group: Lesson 2: What drove the European 'Age of Discovery'?
bio: Broke away from the Catholic Church in 1534.

name: Francis Drake
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Circumnavigated the globe and heavily raided Spanish treasure ships.

name: John Hawkins
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Cousin to Francis Drake and pioneer of the English slave trade.

name: Sir Walter Raleigh
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Organized the first failed English colonization attempt at Roanoke.

name: Chief Powhatan
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Leader of the Powhatan Confederacy who interacted with Jamestown settlers.

name: John Rolfe
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Introduced a profitable tobacco strain to Jamestown.

name: King James I
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Sent an ambassador to the Mughal Empire.

name: Sir Thomas Roe
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Sent to the court of the Mughal Emperor in 1615 to secure trading rights.

name: Emperor Jahangir
group: Lesson 3: Privateers, Companies, and the first English colonies
bio: Wealthy and powerful ruler who permitted early English trade in India.

name: King Charles I
group: Lesson 4: How did the British Civil War create an Imperial Republic?
bio: Believed in the Divine Right of Kings; executed by Parliament in 1649.

name: Oliver Cromwell
group: Lesson 4: How did the British Civil War create an Imperial Republic?
bio: Strict Puritan commander of the New Model Army.

name: John Bradshaw
group: Lesson 4: How did the British Civil War create an Imperial Republic?
bio: Presided over the trial of King Charles I.

name: Martin Noell
group: Lesson 4: How did the British Civil War create an Imperial Republic?
bio: Wealthy merchant, slave trader, and pamphleteer.

name: King Charles II
group: Lesson 4: How did the British Civil War create an Imperial Republic?
bio: Returned to the throne during the Restoration in 1660.

name: Queen Nanny (Nanny of the Maroons)
group: Lesson 5: What was the reality of the Transatlantic Slave Trade?
bio: Led the Jamaican Maroons in a successful guerrilla war against the British.

name: Olaudah Equiano
group: Lesson 5: What was the reality of the Transatlantic Slave Trade?
bio: Formerly enslaved African who published a bestselling autobiography exposing slavery's horrors.

name: Thomas Thistlewood
group: Lesson 5: What was the reality of the Transatlantic Slave Trade?
bio: Jamaican sugar plantation overseer whose diary detailed brutal punishments and slave resistance.

name: King George II
group: Lesson 6: How 'modern' was Britain by 1750? (Synthesis & Assessment)
bio: Governed through a constitutional monarchy via Parliament.

name: Pierre-Jean Grosley
group: Lesson 6: How 'modern' was Britain by 1750? (Synthesis & Assessment)
bio: Observed the extreme contrasts of wealth and poverty in London in 1750.

name: Henry Fielding
group: Lesson 6: How 'modern' was Britain by 1750? (Synthesis & Assessment)
bio: Author who reported on rampant crime and poverty in 1751 London.

name: William Hogarth
group: Lesson 6: How 'modern' was Britain by 1750? (Synthesis & Assessment)
bio: Famous for his 1751 engraving 'Gin Lane' depicting social decay.

name: Kritovoulos of Imbros
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: A 15th-century Greek scholar and historian. Though Greek, he became a subject of the Ottoman Empire and served as an eyewitness and chronicler of the Ottoman siege and capture of Constantinople in 1453.

name: Professor Peter Frankopan
group: Lesson 1: Who held global power in 1450?
bio: A modern historian and author of 'The Silk Roads'. He challenges the Eurocentric myth of 1450, arguing that true global wealth and power were concentrated in the East and along the Silk Road networks, not in Western Europe.

name: Dr. Geoffrey Parker
group: Lesson 3: Why was the Spanish Armada defeated?
bio: A modern revisionist historian who offers a structural view of the Spanish Armada's defeat. He argues that Spain's failure was due to fundamental logistical flaws, poor communication, and bad weather, rather than just English naval superiority.

name: Shashi Tharoor
group: Lesson 4: How did a company conquer a subcontinent?
bio: A modern historian and author of 'Inglorious Empire'. He argues that the British East India Company and similar joint-stock companies were specifically designed to ruthlessly extract wealth and subjugate local populations.

name: Professor Christopher Hill
group: Lesson 5: Why did the English kill their King?
bio: A prominent Marxist historian who championed the 'Political View' of the English Civil War. He argued that the conflict permanently smashed absolute monarchy and laid the groundwork for modern parliamentary democracy.

name: Professor Eric Williams
group: Lesson 5: Why did the English kill their King?
bio: A pioneering historian and author of 'Capitalism and Slavery'. He argued the 'Imperial/Economic View' that the true victors of the Civil War were the Atlantic mercantile class, whose rise to power accelerated the transatlantic slave trade.

name: Professor Roy Porter
group: Lesson 6: Synthesis & Assessment
bio: A modern historian of medicine and society who viewed 1750 Britain as a vibrant, modern, and secular consumer society poised for the Industrial Revolution.

name: Professor J.C.D. Clark
group: Lesson 6: Synthesis & Assessment
bio: A modern historian who challenges the idea of a rapidly modernizing Britain in 1750. He viewed it as an un-modern, traditional 'Ancien Régime' deeply rooted in aristocratic and religious authority.
